subject: Version Control Systems
subtopics: Working Tree Inspection with git status

assessmentTargets.concept: Define Git as a distributed version control system and explain its purpose
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: Git is basically a distributed version control system, which will be helping the developers to keep track about whatever changes they are do
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: Git is basically a distributed version control system, which will be helping the developers to keep track about whatever changes they are do
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to provide a concise definition and purpose of Git as a distributed VCS.

assessmentTargets.concept: Use the appropriate command to verify that Git is installed and identify its version
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: So if you want to know if the Git is installed in your system, then we will be using this particular command called as Git version.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: So if you want to know if the Git is installed in your system, then we will be using this particular command called as Git version.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Prompt the learner to write the command that checks Git installation and explain what output indicates.

assessmentTargets.concept: Explain why Git requires global user name and email configuration before committing changes
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: It is because whenever you are doing any changes in the project and you are saving the changes, to keep track of those changes, to know who has done that particular change, your Git has to know your information.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: It is because whenever you are doing any changes in the project and you are saving the changes, to keep track of those changes, to know who has done that particular change, your Git has to know your information.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to describe the purpose of setting user.name and user.email globally.

assessmentTargets.concept: Demonstrate how to initialize a new local Git repository and describe the result
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: To create a repository in Git, you have to use a command called as git init. So when you use git init, it will tell you that an empty repository has been created.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: To create a repository in Git, you have to use a command called as git init. So when you use git init, it will tell you that an empty repository has been created.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Require the learner to write the git init command and explain what an empty repository means.

assessmentTargets.subtopic: Working Tree Inspection with git status
assessmentTargets.concept: Use git status to list unstaged and staged changes in a repository
assessmentTargets.supportingEvidence: If you want to know what are the changes you have done in your particular project, simply click a command called as git status. It will tell you what are the changes that you have made and which changes have not yet been saved into the repository.
assessmentTargets.evidenceSpan: If you want to know what are the changes you have done in your particular project, simply click a command called as git status. It will tell you what are the changes that you have made and which changes have not yet been saved into the repository.
assessmentTargets.instruction: Ask the learner to execute git status and interpret its output regarding staged vs unstaged changes.

reserveTargets.concept: Recall the three main stages of the Git workflow as introduced in the session
reserveTargets.supportingEvidence: The third stage of your Git, if you remember the workflow.
reserveTargets.evidenceSpan: The third stage of your Git, if you remember the workflow.
reserveTargets.instruction: Prompt the learner to list the three stages of the Git workflow.
